tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

- engine-v2-0: 2/2 available

- Service recommendation-engine Endpoints include 4 pods (2 from each deployment), port 8080

Notes:
- Traffic split is proportional to pod count. Adjust replicas if you want a different ratio, or use an ingress/service mesh for precise weighting.
- Rollback options:

outputSteps.content:
Issue fixed.

Root cause
- The Deployment’s container was started with command: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which fails and caused CrashLoopBackOff. Pod logs showed: “/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found”.

What I changed
- Replaced the Deployment spec to remove the bad command/args and run the default nginx-unprivileged entrypoint.
- Set containerPort: 8080 and added basic readiness/liveness HTTP probes on / (port 8080).
- To avoid field-ownership conflicts, I deleted the broken Deployment and recreated it with the corrected spec.

Current status
- app in crashloop-test is healthy: 1/1 Running (pod: app-7bb599d7b7-8w6td).

If you intended to run a custom command, tell me the correct command/args and I’ll update it. I can also create a Service/Ingress to expose the app if you’d like.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it. Here’s what I found and did:

Root cause
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unusable PVC homepage-pvc (it wasn’t bound yet, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the available StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path), size 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC: homepage-pvc → Bound (StorageClass: standard, Capacity: 1Gi).
- Pod: homepage-pod → Running, container ready, scheduled on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or capacity, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it. Here’s what I found and did:

Root cause
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unusable PVC homepage-pvc (it wasn’t bound yet, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the available StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path), size 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC: homepage-pvc → Bound (StorageClass: standard, Capacity: 1Gi).
- Pod: homepage-pod → Running, container ready, scheduled on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or capacity, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it. Here’s what I found and did:

Root cause
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'sc' not found”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unusable PVC homepage-pvc (it wasn’t bound yet, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using the available StorageClass "standard" (rancher.io/local-path), size 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC: homepage-pvc → Bound (StorageClass: standard, Capacity: 1Gi).
- Pod: homepage-pod → Running, container ready, scheduled on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or capacity, tell me and I’ll adjust the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports: expose 8080.
  - Liveness/readiness probes: HTTP GET path “/” on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready in the orders namespace.
- Service “webapp” points to the pod on port 8080.

How to verify (from your workstation or a debug pod)
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort, depending on your cluster). Would you like me to set that up?

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports: expose 8080.
  - Liveness/readiness probes: HTTP GET path “/” on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready in the orders namespace.
- Service “webapp” points to the pod on port 8080.

How to verify (from your workstation or a debug pod)
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort, depending on your cluster). Would you like me to set that up?

      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      securityContext: {}
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /

          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
            scheme: HTTP

          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
          successThreshold: 1
          failureThreshold: 3
        resources: {}

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- The Deployment’s liveness/readiness probes were checking port 80 and paths (/get_status, /is_ready), causing connection refused.
- The Service was targeting port 80, so traffic wouldn’t reach the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports: expose 8080.
  - Liveness/readiness probes: HTTP GET path “/” on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (port remains 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready in the orders namespace.
- Service “webapp” points to the pod on port 8080.

How to verify (from your workstation or a debug pod)
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- Or port-forward: kubectl -n orders port-forward deploy/webapp 8080:8080 and browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer/NodePort, depending on your cluster). Would you like me to set that up?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include:
  - apiGroup: "" (core), resources: pods, verbs: get, list, watch
  - Kept existing apps/deployments list rule
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already points to this Role and the pod-reader SA, so no change needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: yes
- Or:
  - kubectl --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader get pods -n simple-rbac-setup

If you only want “list” (not get/watch), I can tighten the verbs. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we’ll switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include:

- kubectl auth can-i --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include:
  - apiGroup: "" (core), resources: pods, verbs: get, list, watch
  - Kept existing apps/deployments list rule
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already points to this Role and the pod-reader SA, so no change needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: yes
- Or:
  - kubectl --as system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader get pods -n simple-rbac-setup

If you only want “list” (not get/watch), I can tighten the verbs. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, we’ll switch to a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The nginx Service in namespace web was misconfigured:
  - Selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The container (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
- Evidence:
  - Endpoints were empty before the fix.
  - exec inside the pod showed:
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:80 → failed
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 → 200
  - No Ingress existed in web, so external access wasn’t configured either.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service nginx (namespace web) to select the correct Pods and forward to the correct target port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports: port: 80 name: http targetPort: 8080
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the backing pod: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - In-pod curl to http://nginx/ returns 200

Current Service (summary)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 → targetPort 8080
- Selector: app=nginx
- Endpoints: present

How to verify from your side
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ or curl http://nginx/
- Check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints -n web nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Create an Ingress (assuming ingress-nginx is installed) or change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer. Example Ingress (optional, request if you want me to apply it):
  - spec:
      ingressClassName: nginx
      rules:
      - host: your-hostname.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

Would you like me to expose it externally with an Ingress or a NodePort?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The nginx Service in namespace web was misconfigured:
  - Selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The container (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
- Evidence:
  - Endpoints were empty before the fix.
  - exec inside the pod showed:
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:80 → failed
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 → 200
  - No Ingress existed in web, so external access wasn’t configured either.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service nginx (namespace web) to select the correct Pods and forward to the correct target port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports: port: 80 name: http targetPort: 8080
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the backing pod: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - In-pod curl to http://nginx/ returns 200

Current Service (summary)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 → targetPort 8080
- Selector: app=nginx
- Endpoints: present

How to verify from your side
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ or curl http://nginx/
- Check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints -n web nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Create an Ingress (assuming ingress-nginx is installed) or change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer. Example Ingress (optional, request if you want me to apply it):
  - spec:
      ingressClassName: nginx
      rules:
      - host: your-hostname.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The nginx Service in namespace web was misconfigured:
  - Selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment’s Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
  - Port mismatch: The container (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
- Evidence:
  - Endpoints were empty before the fix.
  - exec inside the pod showed:
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:80 → failed
    - curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 → 200
  - No Ingress existed in web, so external access wasn’t configured either.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service nginx (namespace web) to select the correct Pods and forward to the correct target port:
  - selector: app: nginx
  - ports: port: 80 name: http targetPort: 8080
- Result:
  - Endpoints now show the backing pod: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - In-pod curl to http://nginx/ returns 200

Current Service (summary)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 → targetPort 8080
- Selector: app=nginx
- Endpoints: present

How to verify from your side
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/ or curl http://nginx/
- Check endpoints:
  - kubectl get endpoints -n web nginx

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Create an Ingress (assuming ingress-nginx is installed) or change the Service to NodePort/LoadBalancer. Example Ingress (optional, request if you want me to apply it):
  - spec:
      ingressClassName: nginx
      rules:
      - host: your-hostname.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

Would you like me to expose it externally with an Ingress or a NodePort?

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Additionally, the Service pointed to targetPort 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image typically listens on 8080. That mismatch can cause connection refused even when pods run.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service web-app-service to targetPort 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Ready and Available.
- EndpointSlice now has endpoints for the Service (backends registered).
- Service web-app-service updated to target backend port 8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://web-app-service
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080

If you intended to keep GPU-only scheduling
- Label the node appropriately (for example): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Then add the nodeSelector back to the Deployment.

If you prefer port 80
- Either change the Service back to targetPort 80 and run an image/listener on 80, or reconfigure nginx-unprivileged to listen on 80 (requires appropriate permissions/capabilities). For now, it’s set to 8080 which matches the default for nginx-unprivileged.

deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Additionally, the Service pointed to targetPort 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image typically listens on 8080. That mismatch can cause connection refused even when pods run.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service web-app-service to targetPort 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

Current state
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Ready and Available.
- EndpointSlice now has endpoints for the Service (backends registered).
- Service web-app-service updated to target backend port 8080.

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://web-app-service
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080

If you intended to keep GPU-only scheduling
- Label the node appropriately (for example): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Then add the nodeSelector back to the Deployment.

If you prefer port 80
- Either change the Service back to targetPort 80 and run an image/listener on 80, or reconfigure nginx-unprivileged to listen on 80 (requires appropriate permissions/capabilities). For now, it’s set to 8080 which matches the default for nginx-unprivileged.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Pods weren’t running because the Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Additionally, the Service pointed to targetPort 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image typically listens on 8080. That mismatch can cause connection refused even when pods run.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service web-app-service to targetPort 8080 to match the container’s listening port.

- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Ready and Available.
- EndpointSlice now has endpoints for the Service (backends registered).

How to verify
- From inside the cluster: kubectl -n webshop-frontend run --rm -it curl --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS http://web-app-service
- Or port-forward a pod: kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward deploy/web-app-deployment 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080

If you intended to keep GPU-only scheduling
- Label the node appropriately (for example): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Then add the nodeSelector back to the Deployment.

If you prefer port 80

- kubectl -n multi-container-logging exec -it pod/communication-pod -c web-server -- wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/ (then check logger logs for entries)

results.taskOutput:
All requested multi-tenant configurations have been created and secured according to least-privilege. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access to own namespace (users and their SAs): RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit
  - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa -> edit
  - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa -> edit
  - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa -> edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared (users and their SAs): RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for alice, bob, charlie, and their SAs
- Only cluster admins (system:masters) in staging and prod: RoleBindings to ClusterRole admin for group system:masters
- Note: Using edit (not admin) in dev namespaces follows least privilege while still giving developers full control over typical app resources. If you want them to also manage Roles/RoleBindings in their namespaces, switch to admin.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (limits and requests capped to these totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
- Allow egress to DNS (kube-system/coredns or kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces:
  - Egress allowed only to same namespace and dev-shared
  - Ingress allowed from same namespace; also allowed from dev-shared when needed
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allows ingress from developer namespaces and egress back to them
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC examples:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding dev-shared-view
  - kubectl -n staging get rolebinding staging-admins
- ResourceQuotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-resources
  - Repeat for other namespaces
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - Repeat for other namespaces

Service account token usage (Kubernetes 1.24+)
- To obtain a short-lived token for a developer SA:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Repeat for bob-sa/charlie-sa in their namespaces
- Use that token in a kubeconfig for automation or CI within the allowed scopes

Notes and optional adjustments
- “System services” access currently permits DNS. If workloads need in-cluster API access (https://kubernetes.default.svc), add an egress rule to the API server (labels vary by distro) or to the service ClusterIP as appropriate.
- If you want developers to manage RBAC inside their own namespaces, replace ClusterRole edit with admin in the dev-*-edit RoleBindings.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML bundle of all created resources for your GitOps repo.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested multi-tenant configurations have been created and secured according to least-privilege. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access to own namespace (users and their SAs): RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit
  - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa -> edit
  - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa -> edit
  - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa -> edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared (users and their SAs): RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for alice, bob, charlie, and their SAs
- Only cluster admins (system:masters) in staging and prod: RoleBindings to ClusterRole admin for group system:masters
- Note: Using edit (not admin) in dev namespaces follows least privilege while still giving developers full control over typical app resources. If you want them to also manage Roles/RoleBindings in their namespaces, switch to admin.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (limits and requests capped to these totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
- Allow egress to DNS (kube-system/coredns or kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces:
  - Egress allowed only to same namespace and dev-shared
  - Ingress allowed from same namespace; also allowed from dev-shared when needed
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allows ingress from developer namespaces and egress back to them
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC examples:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding dev-shared-view
  - kubectl -n staging get rolebinding staging-admins
- ResourceQuotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-resources
  - Repeat for other namespaces
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - Repeat for other namespaces

Service account token usage (Kubernetes 1.24+)
- To obtain a short-lived token for a developer SA:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Repeat for bob-sa/charlie-sa in their namespaces
- Use that token in a kubeconfig for automation or CI within the allowed scopes

Notes and optional adjustments
- “System services” access currently permits DNS. If workloads need in-cluster API access (https://kubernetes.default.svc), add an egress rule to the API server (labels vary by distro) or to the service ClusterIP as appropriate.
- If you want developers to manage RBAC inside their own namespaces, replace ClusterRole edit with admin in the dev-*-edit RoleBindings.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML bundle of all created resources for your GitOps repo.

outputSteps.content:
All requested multi-tenant configurations have been created and secured according to least-privilege. Summary of what’s in place:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod

RBAC
- Per-developer ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access to own namespace (users and their SAs): RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit
  - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa -> edit
  - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa -> edit
  - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa -> edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared (users and their SAs): RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for alice, bob, charlie, and their SAs
- Only cluster admins (system:masters) in staging and prod: RoleBindings to ClusterRole admin for group system:masters
- Note: Using edit (not admin) in dev namespaces follows least privilege while still giving developers full control over typical app resources. If you want them to also manage Roles/RoleBindings in their namespaces, switch to admin.

Resource quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (limits and requests capped to these totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

Network policies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress + Egress) in all non-system namespaces: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
- Allow egress to DNS (kube-system/coredns or kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces:
  - Egress allowed only to same namespace and dev-shared
  - Ingress allowed from same namespace; also allowed from dev-shared when needed
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
- dev-shared:
  - Allows ingress from developer namespaces and egress back to them
- staging and prod:
  - Isolated from dev namespaces; only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed

How to verify
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC examples:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding dev-alice-edit
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding dev-shared-view
  - kubectl -n staging get rolebinding staging-admins
- ResourceQuotas:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-resources
  - Repeat for other namespaces
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy
  - Repeat for other namespaces

Service account token usage (Kubernetes 1.24+)
- To obtain a short-lived token for a developer SA:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - Repeat for bob-sa/charlie-sa in their namespaces
- Use that token in a kubeconfig for automation or CI within the allowed scopes

Notes and optional adjustments
- “System services” access currently permits DNS. If workloads need in-cluster API access (https://kubernetes.default.svc), add an egress rule to the API server (labels vary by distro) or to the service ClusterIP as appropriate.
- If you want developers to manage RBAC inside their own namespaces, replace ClusterRole edit with admin in the dev-*-edit RoleBindings.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated YAML bundle of all created resources for your GitOps repo.
